title: Truth and Light; Shared Names Do Not Make the Spirit a Creature
english: … Christ.”

He is the Spirit of truth, as John proclaims the good news from the Saviour: “If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that the Spirit of truth may be with you for ever” (John 14:15-17). And again in his first letter: “And the Spirit is the one who bears witness, because the Spirit is the truth” (1 John 5:6). This is the same manner of speech as the Son’s saying, “I am the truth” (John 14:6).
He is divine Spirit, and the breath of the Almighty, and a lover of mankind, in the words of Job (Job 33:4) and in the words of Moses recalled a few lines above in this chapter (Exodus 31:3).

The Holy Spirit has also been hailed as light, in whom and by whom we are enlightened. So the apostle writes: “that he may give you a spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened” (Ephesians 1:17-18). And David sings: “For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9), that is, in your Son, the radiance of your glory (Hebrews 1:3), your Holy Spirit. And again: “The light of your face has been set as a sign upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:6). For what else could the Spirit be, who proceeds from the Father, that is, from the Light? Of the Father John sang in his first letter, “God is light” (1 John 1:5), and in the Gospel, of the Only-begotten: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world” (John 1:9), and, “I am the light, I am the life” (John 8:12; John 11:25).

Nor is it any wonder if he, being one and remaining always the same, is glorified under different titles. For since his unspeakable Godhead cannot be grasped by the words of mortals, we sing, as far as we are able, of the workings that reach us, and so we make use of different names as well.

But those who champion the doctrine of Macedonius, belonging to their heresy rather than to the truth, see nothing that agrees with the words of Scripture. With words meant to carry the hearer off, they spin the tale, in so many words, that one need not pay attention to homonyms or synonyms or likenesses of wording.

“For with God,” they say, “the name ‘good’ is woven together with ‘one God’; but in the case of the Holy Spirit, ‘one God’ is not yoked to the name ‘good’.” And again: “Man too,” they say, “is written to be good, as when it says, ‘Do good, O Lord, to the good’ (Psalm 125:4), and, ‘The good man brings good things out of his good treasure’ (Matthew 12:35).”

“In the same way,” they say, “even lifeless things are called good by the same name, as when he prophesies, ‘If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land’ (Isaiah 1:19). It is said even of things that, of course, have no substance of their own: ‘It is good to give thanks to the Lord’ (Psalm 92:1).”

“Likewise,” they say, “a man too is called holy, and a grub too is called the power of God, where it is written, ‘The caterpillar, my great power’ (Joel 2:25); and the Saviour as well: ‘The powers of the heavens will be shaken’ (Matthew 24:29).”

Now this, I grant, not paying attention to homonyms and likenesses of wording, makes sense for things that differ in kind and in substance; but not for the Holy Spirit and him whose Spirit he is, nor, indeed, for the Son. For Scripture adds a safeguard of its own to the homonyms or synonyms, and sets beside them the syllable “my” or “your”, or the word “holy” or “good”. That is, it says either, as from God, “my Spirit”, or, as from David and from us, “Your good Spirit will lead me” (Psalm 143:10).

We must therefore be persuaded by what is far more profitable, I mean the scriptural testimonies already cited, and know that the Holy Spirit shares homonymy or synonymy and likenesses of wording with God and with his only-begotten Son, who are hymned under the same names, and not with the creatures, on account of the homonymy that is sometimes found in them.

For even if we were to grant that creatures share some name or word with God, they do not share his substance, nor the working of his power and sanctification. For these things do not belong to them by nature at all. Rather, “good” is ranked by comparison with evil, and “holy” by comparison with sin, or rather with passion. For what is not very evil and sinful, or given to passion, is here called good and holy.

For as wickedness and sin, that is, passion and weakness, are not found in the one Holy Spirit, since he is uncreated, so in none of the things that have come into being are the good, the holy and the powerful present in perfection, but only by participation. And where these are nowhere present in perfection, the uncreated is nowhere present.

For where there is darkness, there is no light at all; and “where there is night, there is no day.” Hence it was said even by Hermes, called Trismegistus: “It is impossible for the good to be in what comes into being; it is in the uncreated alone. And just as a share in all things has been given to matter, so too a share in the good.”
The Holy Spirit, then, is like and equal to the Father’s and …

added_allusions.reason: The Macedonian argument that the name ‘good’ is joined to ‘one God’ rests on “No one is good but one, God” (also Luke 18:19).

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Spirit Holy by Nature; Angels Are Spirits Made, Not Proceeding
english: … the Only-begotten’s Godhead. And from a judgment of these things it is shown that he is by nature holiness and goodness and power, since he is one from the one. For by their wrangling, not even the Son, who is most good and merciful by nature, will be good any longer, since he does not have “one God” joined to his name. Nor indeed will the Father, who loves mankind above all and is wholly merciful, and the Son keep the names of the Godhead just mentioned as their own marks; but by these very names they will be brought down, so to speak, as heretics are in the habit of saying, to us who share the names. Be gracious, Holy Trinity!

“But the Son,” they say, “was begotten together with his goodness and has it inborn, and all else that the Father has.” But the Holy Spirit too proceeded together with it and is good by nature, and has all that God the Father has.

If, then, their dispute were about ordinary matters or the affairs of daily life, it might well have been needful for them at times to make up some tales, and, with a cleverness that is Aristotelian, of course, and with skill in arguments, like Eunomius, to twist the matter round and cast a shadow over the truth. But as it is, Paul teaches: “If you do not believe, neither will you understand” (Isaiah 7:9 LXX), and, “The wisdom of men is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). We must not play the sophist with the sayings about the glorious Spirit, which are greater than human reasonings.

For blame does not harm the Holy Spirit, and the reproaches and gibes of the heretics, on whom wrong thinking has come, go no further than the ear. Rather, those who use such words will labour without end, and will do something like those who try to jeer at this light, which has its strength from the inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6:16), and to defile it with their words.

We must believe that the teaching that comes from the saints has more power to instil conviction than teaching from men. So it befits us to rebuke them, so that they may not, out of excessive goodwill toward their own heresy, drag the divine down, as far as lies with them, among the finished works of creation by their sophistries; nor through these beget a love of perdition in the simpler and less experienced, and lead them on to the desire of greater sins.
Against the heretics who say, “God is spirit” (John 4:24), “and how is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of a spirit?” and again, “Are not the angels, then, from God, and holy, and spirits of God?”

But they set aside what is simple and straightforward and complete, and they fill with ignorance the intent of the sacred words, by which God the Father wills that his Spirit be ranked with him, as the only-begotten Word is, and by which he makes sure that the Spirit is set apart from creation and stands above it; for this reason too he is hailed as thrice holy. And then they say, “How is the Holy Spirit the Spirit of a spirit?”

That this is written has been shown. But the how lies beyond our mind and reason, and even beyond the knowledge of the angels. For as God the Word was begotten from him, since he is Father, so from him and with him the Holy Spirit came forth into light. And in this above all his incomprehensibility is shown: that what appears, and is, impossible for creation is possible with him. Otherwise, what difference would there be between the nature that is uncaused and gives life and the nature that was fashioned and is given life? It is not possible that the Spirit should not be consubstantial and equal in honour with him from whom he is. That is why he is also holy by nature.

“Are not the angels, then,” they say, “from God, and holy, and spirits of God?” They are from God in that they came into being at his command, as all things did; holy once they have been sanctified, as men are; and spirits in that, compared with us, they are bodiless. They have not been called spirits of God, or from God, or proceeding from the Father, or divine, or spirits of truth, or spirits of holiness, but ministering angels and heavenly bodies, because they stand infinitely far from the uncreated Spirit of God and far beneath him. So the experienced apostle writes: “earthly bodies and heavenly bodies” (1 Corinthians 15:40).

For as the spirits of the winds are not on their level, so neither are they on the level of the Holy Spirit of God. For they were created; they did not proceed from the hypostasis of God and Father. They do not regenerate us, they do not make us divine, they do not forgive sins, they do not give life, they do not create, they do not sanctify, they do not judge; rather, they are even judged. For “you,” he says, “will judge even angels” (1 Corinthians 6:3).

Nor are the powers of the heavens like this in themselves. They are not uncircumscribed by place, nor immeasurable in extent. For when Gabriel spoke with Daniel (Daniel 9:21-22), or brought the good news to the Mother of God …

added_allusions.reason: “If you do not believe, neither will you understand” is the Greek of Isaiah 7:9 (the Hebrew and KJV read ‘you shall not be established’); Didymus gives it to Paul. Checked by hand.
“What is impossible for creation is possible with him” echoes “What is impossible with men is possible with God”.
“hailed as thrice holy”: the Trisagion of the seraphim.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u12): retranslated from the Greek. The old draft printed edition numbers (3.30-3.32, '4.') and archaic 'wherefore', split the chapter title across two paragraphs, and garbled many clauses: 'one God does not have a unified nature' (the Son lacks 'one God' joined to his name), 'as it is the custom to speak to heretics', 'the divine which is upon them' (as far as lies with them), 'while they are being sent out, they are simple' (they set aside what is simple), 'impossible to be by Him through creation', 'subtilize themselves' (stand beneath), 'Nor are the powers in them … in places, undefinable'. Isaiah 7:9 (given to Paul) now marked LXX; abbreviated 1 Corinthians references written out; John 4:24, 1 Timothy 6:16 and Daniel 9:21-22 added.

title: The Spirit Fills All Things; Angels Are Bounded and Serve Him
english: … virgin (Luke 1:26-27), he was not in heaven as well in his substance, as he was in thought, but was at that time on earth only. Nor are the angels beyond the bounds of the ages; for “he who makes,” it says, “his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire” (Psalm 104:4).

They do not do a single one of the things done by the Holy Spirit; rather, they serve him, as the archangel Gabriel showed when he ministered to Mary, the Mother of God, and said, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35). Nor, then, is man their temple, as he is the temple of God and of his Spirit and of the only-begotten Son. They are not counted together with God. And the angelic hypostasis is not some single one; the angels are past numbering.

But the Holy Spirit, radiant beyond all things, came forth timelessly, of one nature and one form with it, from the ineffable, super-essential, pre-essential, universal and formless hypostasis of the Father, and he has been named divine. He is one, not multiplied, good, without envy, inaccessible, not to be circumscribed by any thought, infinite in power, unfailing, existing in a way that is his alone. He is by nature holy and the Spirit of God; he is none of the things that exist, but God, who is both in heaven and with us, the cause for all of every good thing. He is present to the whole universe without matter, without form, without change of shape.

Yet he does not depart from his ineffable seat beside the Father. He spreads out everywhere and pervades all, and dwells in all things without being mingled with them. He enters into the thoughts both of us and of those who are invisible to us, and searches all things exactly, though he knows all things (1 Corinthians 2:10). Without a voice he sounds within; he hears souls crying out within in silence, and takes pity on them all in all things without delay, and strengthens them, and gives unspeakable gladness to every nature everywhere. He holds together the frame of this universe and has all things under himself. He enlightens with divine light, and does good by his boundless working and goodness.

Those of better will he leads toward a more perfect goal. Those that are worse, and live amiss, he does not deprive of his kingly protection, which makes for concord and is undivided; instead he sets them longing for, and pondering, the consubstantial Trinity, which supplies every good thing in the universe. He works together with all who labour at what is good, while being set apart above all. So it was that to one of the apostles staying in India, to another in Spain, and to others in other places to the end of the earth, each apportioned his place by him, he imparted his own unerring and unadulterated wisdom. He did not come to this one now and to another later, nor breathe more on one and less on another, but shone upon all at once and upon each, together and distinctly, always alike, just as the Lord, too, said: “I am with you all the days until the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

For surely not — since they themselves transfer to God and Father the theology about the Spirit that stands in John, where he said, “God is Spirit” (John 4:24), saying that it was written so because he is spirit; and further, since it is also written, “The Spirit of our face, Christ the Lord” (Lamentations 4:20 LXX) — will they then number the Father and the Son too, as spirit, with the other ministering spirits? But if this is not so, neither is the Holy Spirit to be thought of with the other spirits. For he is not an archangel. Michael and Gabriel and those like them are archangels; and not even heretics would say that the Holy Spirit of God has been ranked after them.

Where, then, or among what kind of creatures do they think fit to rank him after all? For after God we have been taught from the Scriptures of no other rational nature than that of the many spirits and of bodies such as ours.

Further, they draw a sophistical conclusion from the passages set out above: the Father and the Son are written “true”, but the Spirit “truth”, as if this were out of tune with that. But it is the same, as was shown in the first book, and this does not differ from that.

Against those who say, “Since God the Word is only-begotten, what shall we call the Spirit?” On the Son being attested as only-begotten. The Holy Spirit is one and only; and again, the Son is the Word, the Holy Spirit is the utterance. On comparison; and that there is no example of the incomparable substance.

To this the heretics, who are most intricate and most shifty in speech (whether in mind as well I cannot say, though certainly in this too), strangers to the simpler and truer teaching, turning the same words over again and again, say: “God the Word was called only-begotten because the Holy Spirit is not from the hypostasis of the Father. For if he would not have been called only-begotten, while the …

added_allusions.reason: “The spirit of our face, Christ the Lord”: the Greek of Lamentations 4:20 (πνεῦμα προσώπου ἡμῶν χριστὸς κυρίου); the KJV follows the Hebrew (‘the breath of our nostrils, the anointed of the LORD’). Checked by hand.
Man as the temple of God and of his Spirit.
The Spirit hearing souls that cry out within in silence; cf. the Spirit's groanings too deep for words.
“the other ministering spirits” echoes the angels as “ministering spirits”.
“the Spirit is truth”, set against the Father and Son called “true” (John 17:3; 1 John 5:20); cited earlier in this chapter.
